https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx25.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The rocket component that will strike the Moon is the upper section of a SpaceX Falcon 9 By Kayla Epstein Â and Â Max Matza Published 4 hours ago The Moon has endured countless blows over millions of years. Asteroids and meteors have given the satellite its signature pockmarked surface and network of craters. More recently, it has also experienced impacts from the plucky little probes and landers that Earthbound space agencies have sent hurtling its way. Now on Wednesday, scientists expect the Moon will experience yet another collision, this time from a drifting SpaceX rocket that has been travelling at around 2.43 kilometres per second, or about 5,400mph. The upper stage (section) of one of SpaceX's Falcon 9 rockets will "impact" the Moon on 5 August, according to Nasa's Centre for Near-Earth Object Studies (CNEOS). The US space agency reached the conclusion after independent astronomers, using public data, noted that a portion of the rocket from a January 2025 launch was on an accidental collision course with the Moon. "There is no danger to Earth," said spokesperson Jimi Russell. "Nasa will continue to track the booster for training purposes, as well as later observe the impact site for scientific purposes." Why is space junk such a big problem? SpaceX launched this specific Falcon 9 rocket as part of a US and Japanese mission to carry a pair of lunar landers and scientific equipment to the Moon last year. Part of the Falcon 9 is reusable and designed to return back to Earth for its next mission. But parts of the rocket are shed in space and remain there, stuck in orbit unless they eventually collide with another celestial body. The piece in question is the upper stage of the rocket, and is about the size of a five-storey building, with a weight on Earth of at least 4,000kg (8,800 lbs). Astronomer Bill Gray, who first discovered the trajectory, says the object will land near the Einstein Crater, which is on the part of the Moon that receives daylight and is visible from Earth. He predicts it will create a crater more than 17m (56ft) in diameter. Image source, Getty Images/Nasa Image caption, The Moon's surface bears witness to countless other impacts over a period of millions of years The impending collision - predicted to happen at about 02:35 EDT (06:35 GMT) on Wednesday - is expected to captivate astronomers, both amateur and professional. "It's something really huge smashing into the Moon. It's not remotely dangerous, we can just watch the show," says Dr Matt Bothwell, public astronomer at the University of Cambridge. "It's going to impact and its going to send up a huge plume of dust, maybe 50km into the air or more, and that's going to spread sideways over time," Bothwell said. Given the Moon's lack of atmosphere and far weaker gravitational pull, the moment of impact will be "more impressive than any [similar] explosion on Earth", Bothwell said. Nothing will slow the object down, like the atmosphere would do here on Earth - and nothing will prevent the estimated million kilograms in debris from rocketing up into space. While the impact will not be visible from Earth with the naked eye, people with access to a sophisticated telescope may be able to see a flash radiating off the Moon's surface, Bothwell said. More significant would be the educative potential of the impact, Bothwell noted. He said this moment would present a unique opportunity to study what happens when an object hits the Moon. Scientists are therefore gearing up to watch the event closely. Big telescopes in the Americas, plus Nasa's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and South Korea's Danuri probe, will track the flash, plume and new crater, and a citizenâscience project is signing up keen amateurs to film the impact too. By catching the dust plume in action, astronomers hope to turn this accidental crash into a useful experiment. Watching how much material gets thrown up, how high it goes and how it falls back should sharpen their models of lunar impacts â and even give clues about what lies just beneath the surface at the impact site, where fresh subsurface material will be exposed for the first time. Figure caption, The space junk clean-up (2018) Bothwell, the astronomer, also said the collision would provide a cautionary tale about the issue of ever-accumulating, human-made space clutter. "I think more people should be more worried about space debris," Bothwell said. "Every single year we put more stuff in orbit. Sometimes the satellites just collide, and they shatter into more pieces. I think there's a worry about a runaway cascade, if we put so much stuff in orbit." According to the European Space Agency (ESA), there are around 54,000 objects floating in space that measure larger than 10cm. In total, humans have launched about 17,000 tonnes of objects into space since the Space Age began in 1957. The last dead rocket to impact the Moon was in 2022, when the Chinese Long March 3C upper stage from the 2014 Chang'e 5âT1 mission hit the far side of the Moon - which faces away from Earth. Decades earlier, Nasa launched objects into the Moon on purpose, in order to collect data for the Apollo missions. Photograph: Reuters Ukraine Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’ US president says Zelenskyy ‘more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin’ after ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses Europe live – latest updates Jennifer Rankin in Brussels and agencies Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.01 EDT First published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 02.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump has called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace”, while renewing his criticism of Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy after an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine collapsed. Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries ⁠after Zelenskyy said that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire abruptly declared by Trump last week, one that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to. Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses Read more In an interview with the Newsmax news outlet aired on Thursday, the US president said: “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace. “There are a lot ‌of targets you can ‌hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, ‌diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he’s not doing a good service for the world.” Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since last week, when Trump eased sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel on to global markets. Zelenskyy criticised the agreement, which was widely interpreted as an attempt to curb high fuel prices before the US midterm election, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than four and a half years ago. US efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress. Trump repeated to Newsmax his views of the two leaders involved in the conflict. “I’m not a big fan of Zelenskyy,” Trump said. “I think they actually both would like to see it ⁠end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin.” Arriving in Brussels to meet EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy did not comment on Trump’s latest remarks. He said he was “so thankful that we have such huge support from the EU” and its leaders, whom he described as “real leaders”. He went on to say that Ukraine wanted to end the war as quickly as possible, but “we don’t see now signals from [the] Russian side that they are ready for this”. View image in fullscreen Volodymyr Zelenskyy, centre, with ‘real leaders’ Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa, arriving at a summit of EU leaders in Brussels. Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/Reuters Kyiv’s relationship with Washington was strained further this week when Ukraine said Starlink services had been restricted , in effect hobbling Ukrainian drone strike missions and crucial air defences with a flick of the switch. During a visit to London this week, the Ukrainian president said the sudden restriction of Starlink had left him feeling personally betrayed by Trump and lamented losing a partner. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses Read more The British defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on Thursday that his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that the vital satellite communications system had been restored. In an interview with the BBC, he said it was unclear what had caused the disruption, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.” Amid growing doubts about long-term US commitment to Ukraine, European leaders declared their support for Zelenskyy. Standing alongside the Ukrainian leader in Brussels, the European Council president, António Costa, said Ukraine could “count on us not only to support you in war” but also in the path to negotiating EU membership. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire, “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions, adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.” The promise of further European sanctions against Russia comes weeks after the EU lifted sanctions against two prominent Russian oligarchs at the request of France and Luxembourg. View image in fullscreen Ukrainian rescuers work at the site of a Russian missile strike on a residential building in Kyiv on 14 October. Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPA After meeting Zelenskyy, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said it was “crucial” that Ukraine received “all the means necessary to protect itself”. The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, posted online: “I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelenskyy: YOU ARE NOT ALONE.” As Zelenskyy met Macron in Brussels, he said that the Kremlin had “launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure” in the city of Lutsk, which caused blackouts. The Kremlin, meanwhile, accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries. Emily Alff/Missourian Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save COLUMBIA — Heavy rain Thursday led to the cancellation of this year’s Decorate the District event for the first time in recent history. The Mizzou Homecoming Committee said the event will not be rescheduled. Decorate the District is an at least 20-year-old Mizzou Homecoming tradition. Typically, Mizzou student organizations paint storefront murals and window paintings at businesses in downtown Columbia ahead of the Homecoming weekend. The paintings are completed in one day by students in the organizations and can be viewed through the weekend. Decorate the District is one of many traditions and activities that students can participate in during Homecoming. Amid the cancellation and heavy rainfall, the National Weather Service issued a flood warning for northeastern Boone County, in effect from Saturday evening until further notice. The weather service predicts the Missouri River could go over the flood stage at Boonville, rising to 23.8 feet by Monday, according to its website. This could affect Easley River Road and Smith Hatchery Road. If the Missouri River rises to 25 feet, flooding could occur on agricultural land and secondary roads. Backwater flooding on Perche Creek causes flooding in McBaine. As of Thursday morning, the flood stage was at 12 feet. The river is expected to rise above the flood stage Sunday morning. It is expected to rain through Thursday and dry up by Friday, KOMU 8 meteorologists said. Across the two days, the anticipated rainfall is 1½ to 2 inches. As of Thursday morning, there have been no reports of flooding in Columbia, said Matt Beitscher, the lead meteorologist at the National Weather Service St. Louis. “The only real impacts we are expecting in Boone County would be at the worst minor river flooding along the Missouri River,” Beitscher said. Shakespeare’s Pizza, a staple of downtown, has been involved with Decorate the District for more than 20 years, said general manager Toby Epstein. Success! Epstein said the storefront murals signal to the community that Homecoming weekend is about to begin. “Anytime there is anything new or different or interesting going on in the downtown area, it’s going to bring interest from the community,” he said. Epstein said this is the busiest weekend for the business, and he added that Homecoming is always something to look forward to. Her Campus, a student organization that publishes digital articles and is led by women, was also planning to participate in Decorate the District this year. The organization would have decorated Bluestem Missouri Crafts, which it painted murals for last year, Her Campus President Faith Scheerer said. “We had a lot of volunteers that were looking forward to it, so it was upsetting to know that it was an opportunity that was missed,” Scheerer said. Scheerer also said Decorate the District is a good opportunity to connect the university with the city. Her Campus will participate in the Homecoming Parade with its float on Saturday. For some organizations, this was their first experience with Homecoming festivities, including the Uzbek Students Organization. The group, which promotes culture and cuisine from Uzbekistan, planned to decorate Cafe Poland this year. Akbar Kamoldinov, president of the Uzbek Students Organization, said he was looking forward to having another opportunity to promote Uzbekistan’s culture. “I was hoping to add some cultural elements to the mural,” Kamoldinov said.
